articles.title: Elon Musk Is Spending More Than $275 Million on the Midterm Elections. Did We Always Have This Much Money in Politics—And Is This Even Legal?
articles.content:
Since July, trillionaire Elon Musk has spent $276 million dollars on the upcoming midterm elections, according to the New York Times. He directed that astonishing amount of money to both his super political action committee (PAC) and Republican groups in a bid to stave off what is expected to be major losses for the party this fall.
Much of this money, about $158 million, went to the Senate Leadership Fund in an effort to maintain a majority in that chamber of Congress. Another big outlay, $76 million, went to Musk’s super PAC, which will spend the cash on canvassing for candidates in seven Senate races and dozens of House ones.
And that’s just since July. All in all, he has spent roughly $366 million dollars on the 2025–2026 election cycle. This isn’t the first time Musk has made influential campaign contributions either. He spent more than $290 million on the 2024 election, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings—more than any other donor.
As of the latest FEC filings from July, PACs from all parties had raised $8.3 billion and spent $6.5 billion during the 2025–2026 election cycle. (The FEC filing deadline is coming up on Oct. 15, 2026, so these numbers are even higher now.) It’s hard to believe that it’s legal for people like Musk to spend these staggering amounts to influence elections, but thanks to a landmark 2010 Supreme Court ruling, it is.
Ahead, we spoke with politics and election-law experts Jen Heerwig, PhD, Donald Tobin, JD, and Alex Keena, PhD, to understand this consequential (and controversial) court case. Read on to learn more about the influence of money in politics and how this case changed campaign spending.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more election news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
In inflation-adjusted terms, the elections of 2020 broke all records: Nearly $19 billion was spent on the presidential race and congressional races combined, says Heerwig, an associate professor of sociology at SUNY-Stony Brook who studies political contributions by American corporate elites. In 2016, that number was less than $10 billion. “It’s unusual to see the cost of elections nearly double in the space of four years,” she says.
One reason for this increase is the gradual influx of super PACs, Heerwig explains. “In 2016, over $1 billion was spent by super PACs. In 2020, over $2 billion was spent by these groups.” A large proportion of this money goes to political advertising, which is getting more expensive every year.
That said, the composition of spending in our elections had been changing even before the explosion of money in 2020. And as you’ll see coming up, there’s a reason why super PACs have become such an important driver of election spending.
The driving force behind this substantial shift in campaign contributions was a 2010 Supreme Court case, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which allowed corporations to spend unlimited sums of money to support or oppose a candidate running for federal office.
“Previously, corporations had to establish a PAC, which could only spend $5,000 giving to a particular candidate under the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971,” according to Keena, an associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University who focuses on money in politics and elections. “The Supreme Court said that part of the law was unconstitutional because it violated the ‘political speech’ rights of corporations.”
Essentially, the Supreme Court reasoned that corporations should have the First Amendment right to speak in elections. “After Citizens United, a private company could decide to make an advertisement to support the candidacy of, say, Donald Trump or a candidate running for the U.S. House or Senate,” Heerwig says. “Since there are no limits on independent expenditures, a company could spend unlimited amounts to support its favored candidates, so long as it did so on its own.”
The ruling has had a predictable influence on our elections. “Since the Citizens United ruling, super PACs have gradually become more important in election spending,” Heerwig says.
The Citizens United ruling created a new type of PAC—a super PAC—that can give unlimited money but cannot directly “coordinate” with a campaign. “In practice, this requirement is unenforced,” Keena explains. “For example, Elon Musk created a super PAC to help Trump win in 2024, and he was in frequent contact with the Trump campaign and even appeared on stage with Trump when he was a candidate.”
Interestingly, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission began in the lower courts as a case about what kinds of information must be disclosed by entities making political advertisements and communications, Heerwig explains. But the U.S. Supreme Court’s consideration of the case revolved around the ban on corporate independent spending—contributions made directly from company treasuries to influence elections, like a political advertisement made to support or oppose a candidate for the U.S. House or Senate, she notes.
This massive shift in contributions makes candidates, campaigns and political parties more reliant on corporate and monied interests, Keena says. “The increase in money being spent means candidates have to spend more of their time asking the rich for donations, and in response, the political parties have become more responsive to the interests of the wealthy and special interests that support them,” he explains.
The result? Congress now gives preferential treatment to the ideas and policies favored by the donor class and makes symbolic overtures to ordinary citizens rather than offering substantive representation, Keena says.
Super PAC spending tends to target the most competitive races, where spending even a small amount of money may be more meaningful, Heerwig says. “In these races, we’ve seen super PACs inundate media markets with advertisements of all types—online, print, television, etc.,” she explains.
Yes, it’s totally legal for Elon Musk to channel hundreds of millions of dollars into our elections through his super PAC. “The courts view this money as a constitutional right,” Keena says. “All Americans are entitled to spend as much as they want on election advertising and communications.”
However, Musk’s super PAC can’t coordinate with official candidate committees, Heerwig says. But that restriction doesn’t have much bite these days. “In practice, we know that super PACs can and do coordinate with candidates, and our chief federal election watchdog, the Federal Election Commission, has not meaningfully intervened,” she explains.
It’s important to recognize that Elon Musk could spend unlimited dollars on the midterms prior to Citizens United as long as he did not coordinate with any candidate, says Tobin, an election and tax law professor and former dean of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law. What Citizens United did was allow Musk to make such contributions through a corporate form.
“In reality, it had no serious impact on an individual’s ability to spend unlimited funds,” he explains. “It just made it easier because Musk can create an independent expenditure PAC and he can just contribute to that PAC.”
Yes, it’s possible that the Citizens United ruling will be reversed at some point, Keena says.
If (or when) the membership of the Supreme Court changes (such as through death, resignation or future expansion) or when societal attitudes change, “future courts could reverse this ruling,” Keena says. “Otherwise, reversing it would require a constitutional amendment.”
Alternatively, Congress could pass legislation creating a different regulatory system for campaign contributions, Tobin says.
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, keep an eye out for the signs that big money is at play. Keena recommends looking at who is giving money to the candidates as well as the super PAC money being spent to support them. “This money creates relationships of obligations between politicians and their financiers, and it previews what types of policies a politician might support or oppose in office,” he explains.
If you live in a state or district with a competitive race, Heerwig suggests paying very careful attention to the disclaimer that appears at the end of political advertisements. “If the advertisement does not explicitly contain the endorsement of the named candidate, then it’s an ad that’s been funded by a third-party group, likely a super PAC,” she explains. “Stay vigilant about fact-checking the claims coming from these groups.”

articles.title: This Food Is Actually Healthier as a Leftover—Can You Guess What It Is?
articles.content:
In my house, we try to have a home-cooked dinner at least five nights a week. That said, we’ve learned that the only way this is remotely achievable is to choose at least one meal that makes enough to eat twice—once fresh out of the oven or off the stovetop, and again as leftovers later in the week. A lot of the time, this is soup. (We’re a big soup household.) But the second-most-common dish we have on leftovers night is one that’s actually healthier for you to eat one or two days after cooking.
Yes, you heard that right. There’s one beloved food that’s better for you if you cook it and then pop it in the fridge for a day or two before eating it. What kind of sorcery is this? The wonderful kind!
Keep reading to find out what this magical food is—and what kind of special alchemy happens in your fridge when it spends the night in there.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food news, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Ever heard of lasagna? Spaghetti and meatballs? Penne a la vodka? I could go on—I do love my pasta. And that’s a good thing because pasta is the food I’m talking about. It’s actually much healthier when it’s eaten as leftovers, and it’s all because of what happens to the starch molecules that make up the pasta during both the cooking and cooling processes.
“When pasta cooks, its starch granules absorb water, and [they] swell,” explains Jordan Langhough, a registered dietitian and certified personal trainer in Charlotte, North Carolina. “This process makes it easier for your body to break down the starch quickly and turn it into glucose.”
But then, as your hot pasta cools, something else happens. “When it cools, those starch molecules go through a process called retrogradation: They reorganize into a tighter, more crystalline structure that your digestive enzymes can’t break down as easily,” Langhough says. This new structure that’s formed is called resistant starch—and it is the key to all the potential health benefits you can get from leftover pasta.
“Resistant starch acts more like fiber than a carb in the body,” says Langhough. What does that mean? When you eat simple carbs, like white bread or cookies, your body immediately breaks them down, sending glucose (aka sugar) straight into your bloodstream, and that can cause a host of problems. Fiber, on the other hand, travels through your digestive system without being broken down, which leads to a variety of possible perks, including the following.
During digestion, resistant starch isn’t broken down in the stomach like simpler carbs are. Instead, explains Langhough, it travels to the large intestine, where it acts as a prebiotic, or a food that nourishes the beneficial bacteria that live there. This allows the healthy bacteria in your gut to thrive. Studies have shown that people with a healthier, more diverse microbiome have lower cholesterol levels, higher fitness levels and greater longevity than those who don’t have as many good bugs living in their gut. That’s because these bacteria influence everything from digestion to disease prevention.
On the flip side, if your microbiome is overrun by bad bugs, you can experience digestive difficulties, an increased risk of inflammatory bowel diseases, fatigue, mood changes and more, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The bottom line: You want your gut microbiome to be as healthy as possible, and eating foods rich in resistant starch is an excellent way to support that goal.
Resistant starch reduces the glycemic impact of the meal, or how quickly the food causes your blood sugar to rise, says Langhough. While hot pasta contains simple starches that are broken down quickly, causing a rapid rise, the resistant starch in leftover pasta is not broken down at all, slowing the spike that your meal creates.
This is a big deal for people with diabetes who are trying to avoid blood-sugar spikes. According to one study in the Journal of Diabetes Investigation, resistant starch seems to lower post-meal blood-sugar levels, making it a promising part of medical nutrition therapy for type 2 diabetes.
That said, avoiding blood-sugar spikes is smart for everyone. Frequent extreme spikes and dips in those levels can contribute to increased inflammation, low energy, poor sleep, irritability and possibly even an increased risk of cancer, according to a 2025 review. You also tend to feel hungry again after a spike and drop in blood sugar, which can lead to snacking and subsequent weight gain. It’s best to keep your blood sugar as steady as possible.
“Over time, regularly eating resistant starch has been linked to a greater sense of fullness after eating,” Langhough says. That’s primarily because it travels through the GI tract without breaking down, so you’ll feel fuller for longer, potentially delaying your next meal or snack and reducing your overall food intake for the day.
The result: In a study in the journal Nature Metabolism, people who used resistant starch as a dietary supplement for eight weeks while eating a balanced diet lost an average of 6.2 pounds. In addition to the satiety boost, researchers suspect this is because resistant starch reduces inflammation and nourishes the gut microbiome, both of which contribute to a healthier body weight.
According to a review in Nutrition Research, consuming resistant starch helps lower both total cholesterol and LDL (bad) cholesterol levels, which can reduce your risk of heart disease and stroke. Again, this comes back to your microbiome: The resistant starch feeds your good gut bugs, which then produce compounds called short-chain fatty acids that help the body break down harmful fats instead of absorbing and storing them.
And, of course, enjoying your pasta with other heart-healthy foods like veggies and olive oil will further support this perk … as opposed to slathering it in a creamy, cheesy sauce.
To maximize how much resistant starch is formed, Langhough suggests refrigerating pasta overnight. “The pasta needs to cool down significantly,” she says. “Some retrogradation begins at room temperature, but you get the most resistant-starch formation after chilling it overnight in the fridge.”
That said, don’t seal it up in a storage container too quickly. Langhough recommends waiting around 30 minutes to let the steam escape and get a jump-start on cooling before putting it in a wide, shallow container in the fridge—if you put hot food in a deep container, the middle may remain in the “danger zone” for bacterial growth longer than you want it to.
But, she adds, “from a food-safety standpoint, you don’t want cooked pasta sitting out for more than two hours at room temperature, so [don’t] delay much beyond that.”
Don’t worry—you don’t have to eat that pasta cold unless you want to. “Because retrogradation is partially irreversible, a meaningful amount of resistant starch remains even after reheating,” says Langhough.
In fact, cooking, cooling and reheating pasta may actually be the best approach for maximizing the perks. One study in the journal Foods found that reheated pasta produced a smaller blood-sugar spike after eating than both hot, freshly cooked pasta and cold pasta.
Some people are wary of eating leftover pasta dishes for fear of something called reheated rice syndrome, which, as the name implies, can also happen when reheating rice. A form of food poisoning caused by the bacteria B. cereus, it can lead to vomiting, diarrhea and, in rare cases, more serious illness. However, the name is a bit of a misnomer, since it’s not the reheating process that causes the bacteria to form the spores that make you sick. Instead, they form and produce toxins if the rice or pasta is left at room temperature for too long during the preparation or cooling process. The problem is that these spores are heat-resistant, explains Langhough, so once they have formed, reheating your leftovers won’t do anything to kill them.
As technical and worrisome as this sounds, here’s the only thing you really need to know: Make sure your pasta is in the fridge within two hours of cooking it, ideally sooner. The less time it spends at room temperature, the better. If you do that, you should be able to avoid these risks.
Yes! A few, in fact, as you’ll see below.
Look, we know you probably won’t stop eating hot, fresh pasta altogether—and as long as you’re eating it as part of a balanced meal, you don’t need to. But consider this your go-ahead to enjoy it for a second (or third) night. Your body will thank you.

  • Rice and potatoes: “The same principle applies,” says Langhough. “Cook them, cool them in the fridge, and they develop significantly more resistant starch than when eaten hot.”
  • Beans and lentils: “These are naturally high in resistant starch, and they get an additional boost when cooled,” Langhough says.
  • Oats: Overnight oats aren’t just convenient—they also contain more resistant starch than their hot counterparts, making them a “particularly blood-sugar-friendly breakfast,” per Langhough.

Look, we know you probably won’t stop eating hot, fresh pasta altogether—and as long as you’re eating it as part of a balanced meal, you don’t need to. But consider this your go-ahead to enjoy it for a second (or third) night. Your body will thank you.

articles.title: Chihuahuas Are Made Up of *What* Kind of Animal?! This New Study Is Totally Wild
articles.content:
Folks, a new study has confirmed what we all expected: Chihuahuas are a breed all their own. The feisty little spitfires and national dogs of Mexico were the focus of research published this summer in Nature Communications, and it turns out they have a certain wild-animal DNA that will make so much sense once you hear it.
If you’ve ever parented a Chihuahua or happen to have crossed one of their paths, you know these attitude-heavy canines pack a lot of punch in their tiny bodies. Ahead, I’ll walk you through the results of this study and explain how the heck researchers even determined this mind-blowing revelation. Read on to learn more about this fascinating study.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more pet news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Your ferocious but lovable little lap dog has coyote blood coursing through his veins! Researchers confirmed this astounding fact while they were studying the effectiveness of a certain type of genetic sequencing that is way too complicated to go into here, but the results are pretty cool regardless.
Because coyotes are native to North America, the study authors keyed in on dogs that have been present in the Americas for hundreds of years, before European contact, to test a new genomic sequencing algorithm. This included the Chihuahua and a dog called the Xoloitzcuintli (aka the Xolo), a hairless breed that also has its origins in Mexico. And yep, both breeds share DNA with the coyote.
It has to do with selective breeding. Earlier research has found that nearly all dogs smaller than 15 pounds share a certain genetic marker on one particular chromosome (CFA15). This shared gene, which has to do with insulin production, led researchers to determine that early on in the domestication process—we’re talking thousands of years ago—humans began deliberately selecting for small dogs.
We’re not sure if that means the ancients also liked lap dogs, or whether the relentless little yappers were bred for another purpose, like alerting the group to invaders. Nor did this study determine how much coyote DNA remains in today’s Chihuahuas, though earlier research put the figure at roughly 4%. It’s also not known if cross-breeding between coyotes and domestic dogs was deliberate. But we do know that humans selected for smaller dogs at some point in the past.
If you’ve ever been around a Chihuahua, you know they have a lot of personality packed into their tiny bodies. But according to the American Kennel Club (AKC), they tend to be reserved at first, which aligns with their skittish coyote brethren.
Chihuahuas are fiercely loyal and protective of their families, and it turns out that coyotes are too. You may think of coyotes as solitary figures, especially if you live in an urban environment, but they often live in monogamous pairs and family groups and will defend their territory. Coyotes even exhibit play behavior like domestic dogs.
Coyotes are also self-preservationists: According to Project Coyote, a conservation group, the wild animals tend to “bluff charge” when confronted rather than aggressively engaging a threat directly. Kind of sounds like a Chihuahua, who wants you to know she’s tough but also understands the limitations of her tiny size.
According to the AKC, even though they are small, Chihuahuas do best with training so they don’t “rule your household like a little Napoleon.” Start your relationship right with puppy classes, and make sure to provide these intelligent dogs with engaging things to do.
Chihuahuas enjoy short walks to avoid overexertion, or can be exercised easily with a ball or toy in smaller spaces like apartments. Even though they enjoy sitting in your lap for hours (unlike a coyote!), all dogs need stimulation to stave off boredom and be happy. Chihuahuas are a natural at obedience training and canine sports, according to the AKC.

articles.title: Pumpkin Spice Lattes in Real Pumpkins Are Going Viral—Here’s How to Get One for Yourself
articles.content:
It’s officially pumpkin spice season, and you know what that means! Cozy sweaters, pumpkin patches and, of course, that first glorious sip of a pumpkin spice latte. Whether you’re the type to order one the second it hits the menu or you’ve already lost count of how many you’ve had this fall (no judgment!), there’s just something about a PSL that makes the season feel complete. But just when you thought your favorite fall drink couldn’t get any more festive, the internet said, “Hold my pumpkin.”
That’s right! A viral fall tradition is making its annual comeback on TikTok and Instagram, and it’s giving everyone’s favorite seasonal coffee order an adorable twist. You might have seen this trend pop up on your feed in previous years, but if you’ve never actually tried it yourself, consider this your sign to finally get in on the fun. And the best part? You don’t need to be a social media influencer to join the pumpkin party.
Read on to find out what this viral pumpkin spice latte trend is all about, how to try it yourself and a few ways you can give your typical PSL a festive fall makeover.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, food, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
@macyhorman0 Happy September 1st! 🤎 Pumpkin Spice Latte, but make it festive!! #starbucks #fallseason #fallvibes #starbucksdrinks #pumpkinseason ♬ orijinal ses – gilmore🍂☕️
People are bringing their own hollowed-out mini pumpkins to Starbucks and asking baristas to pour their pumpkin spice lattes straight into them. Some lucky customers have even gotten the full treatment, complete with a swirl of whipped cream and a sprinkle of pumpkin spice on top.
But don’t expect every Starbucks to be on board. Many baristas turn down these requests because of food-safety rules. After all, a pumpkin isn’t exactly a standard coffee cup.
Luckily, there’s an easy workaround. Bring your own clean, hollowed-out mini pumpkin and order your PSL as usual. If the barista can’t serve it directly in your pumpkin, simply pour the drink in yourself after picking up your order. You can also ask for whipped cream on the side to give your pumpkin cup that picture-perfect finishing touch. Just like that, you’ve got yourself a viral-worthy fall drink!
Drinking a PSL out of a real pumpkin might look cute on camera, but it comes with a few potential problems. For one, pumpkins can carry dirt and bacteria on their skin. If they aren’t properly washed and hollowed out, you could end up with more than just pumpkin spice in your latte.
And it’s not just your own health that cafes like Starbucks have to worry about. Bringing a raw pumpkin behind the counter could introduce dirt, bacteria and other contaminants into an area where drinks are prepared. There’s also the risk of cross-contamination if the pumpkin touches equipment or food-preparation surfaces. That’s why baristas may refuse to fill your pumpkin directly. They have food-safety standards to follow, and a mystery gourd from someone’s kitchen isn’t exactly an approved coffee cup!
Hot drinks are another concern. Pouring a steaming PSL into a raw pumpkin can soften the flesh and potentially cause leaks. And if your pumpkin has been sitting around since your last carving session, that’s a definite no-go. Cut pumpkins can spoil and grow bacteria or mold over time.
Your best bet? Use a fresh pumpkin that’s been thoroughly cleaned and hollowed out right before serving. Better yet, pop a small food-safe cup inside the pumpkin and pour your latte into that. You’ll get the same adorable fall aesthetic without having to wonder whether your pumpkin is actually safe to drink from.
A pumpkin cup isn’t the only way to make your PSL feel a little more special. Here are a few easy upgrades worth trying on your next coffee run.
Who knew there were so many ways to make pumpkin spice season even better?

A pumpkin cup isn’t the only way to make your PSL feel a little more special. Here are a few easy upgrades worth trying on your next coffee run.

  • Add pumpkin cream cold foam. Top your iced PSL with pumpkin cream cold foam for an extra creamy sip.

articles.title: This Is the Scariest Movie from the Year You Were Born
articles.content:
Some birthdays come with balloons and cake. Others come with masked murderers, creepy dolls and things that go bump in the night. OK, not literally (thank goodness), but have you ever wondered about the scariest movie that came out the year you were born? There’s something delightfully creepy, not to mention deliciously evil, about knowing which horror movie was giving everyone goosebumps the year you arrived.
To find out, we rounded up the scariest horror movies released each year from 1950 to 2005. We looked at Rotten Tomatoes’ best horror movie rankings, along with critical reviews, audience reactions and each film’s reputation for delivering serious scares. After all, a movie can earn rave reviews without making you want to check under your bed. (And where’s the fun in that?)
Ready to meet the movie that was terrifying audiences the year you were born? Read on to find your birth year’s scariest film. Just don’t blame us if you end up sleeping with the lights on.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment, news, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
From sinister black-and-white thrillers to terrifying supernatural encounters, horror movies have been giving audiences nightmares for generations. Here are the scariest movies released each year from 1950 to 2005.
If there’s one horror movie that deserves a permanent spot in the nightmare hall of fame, it’s The Exorcist (1973). Directed by William Friedkin, the film follows a 12-year-old girl named Regan who becomes possessed by a demon, leaving her desperate mother to seek help from two priests. Sounds creepy enough, right? Well, audiences in 1973 were reportedly fainting and feeling sick in theaters. The movie became a massive box-office hit and made history as the first horror film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture. And more than 50 years later, it’s still giving people the chills. In fact, The Exorcist took the No. 1 spot in a Rotten Tomatoes poll of the scariest horror movies ever made, earning 19% of the votes. It also holds a 78% critics score and an impressive 87% audience score on the site.
Of course, The Exorcist isn’t the only horror movie that’s earned a reputation for keeping viewers up at night. Hereditary (2018), a deeply unsettling story about a grieving family with some seriously disturbing secrets, came in second in the Rotten Tomatoes poll. Other fan favorites include The Conjuring (2013), which follows paranormal investigators tackling a terrifying haunting, and The Shining (1980), in which Jack Nicholson’s character slowly loses his mind at an isolated hotel. And who could forget The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974)? That one made us think twice about taking a wrong turn on a road trip.
Think you can sit through any horror movie without flinching? Sinister (2012) might have you eating those words (and hiding behind a pillow). Directed by Scott Derrickson, this supernatural nightmare stars Ethan Hawke as a true-crime writer who moves his family into a house with a gruesome past. When he discovers a box of disturbing home movies, things go from creepy to downright terrifying.
And there’s science to back up the scares! The Science of Scare Project crowned Sinister the scariest movie of all time, giving it a whopping 96 out of 100 on its Scare Score. Researchers monitored viewers’ heart rates and found that the film sent their pulses racing, with heart rates peaking at 131 beats per minute. Yikes! Horror experts at Bloody Disgusting have also highlighted the film’s reputation, while Dread Central reported that it reclaimed the top spot in the study’s 2025 rankings. Of course, everyone’s fear factor is different, but when a movie can make your heart race like that, you might want to leave a light on. Just saying.
